Dietary carbohydrate-to-protein ratio governs the contribution of insulin-AKT-TSC2 signaling to hepatic mTORC1 activation The results above provide evidence that amino acid concentrations dictate the role of insulin signaling in the activation of hepatic mTORC1. Given the macronutrient differences between the CTL and chow diets (Fig. 3b), we sought to determine whether the dietary carbohydrate-to-protein ratio dictates the dominant route to mTORC1 activation in liver tissue by refeeding a high carbohydrate, low protein (HC-LP) diet. The formulated HC-LP diet derives 80% calories from carbohydrate and 10% from protein (Fig. 3b), as previous studies have demonstrated that short-term feeding of a 10% protein diet does not elicit markers of protein restriction66. Following one-hour refeeding with the HC-LP diet, hepatic mTORC1 signaling was induced by approximately seven-fold in L-TSC2-WT mice, with only modest and signiﬁcantly reduced induction in L-TSC-5A livers (Fig. 4a). Importantly, insulin levels in response to acute feeding were similar between the HC-LP (Fig. 4b) and chow diets (Fig. S2d). Thus, taken together with the primary hepatocyte experiments, these results demonstrate that lower dietary protein content renders AKT-mediated phosphorylation of TSC2 the primary route to feeding-induced hepatic mTORC1 signaling. While there are no known direct effects of mTORC1 signaling on hepatic or systemic glucose metabolism, mTORC1-mediated feedback mechanisms can, theoretically inﬂuence the insulin responsiveness of a given tissue10,11,29,67–70. Interestingly, accompanying the decrease in mTORC1 stimulation, the induction of AKT activation was more pronounced in the L-TSC2-5A livers with HC-LP refeeding (Fig. 4a), despite insulin levels being equivalent to those in L-TSC2-WT mice (Fig. 4b). Measurements of direct targets of AKT, including PRAS40 and GSK3α/ β phosphorylation, further demonstrated pronounced AKT activation in the L-TSC2-5A livers(Fig. S4a), indicative of enhanced hepatic insulin sensitivity. To test whether fasted or insulin-stimulated hepatic mTORC1 activation was altered in L-TSC2−5A compared to -WT mice under conditions of obesity and hyperinsulinemia, we assessed liver signaling in fasted L-TSC2-WT and −5A males treated with vehicle or insulin after 10 weeks on an HFD. Fasting hepatic mTORC1 activation was not signiﬁcantly different between L-TSC2-WT and -5A mice (Fig. 6g). Importantly, as detected in lean mice (Fig. 2a), mTORC1 induction by exogenous administration of insulin was impaired in diet-induced obese L-TSC2-5A compared to -WT mice, but this was not associated with signiﬁcantly increased AKT activation (Fig. 6g). Given that skeletal muscle mTORC1 signaling was signiﬁcantly higher in obese compared to lean mice (Fig. S5f), we measured skeletal muscle signaling effects in the L-TSC2-WT and -5A mice fed a HFD. L-TSC2-WT and -5A skeletal muscle remained insulin sensitive following 10 weeks of HFD feeding, and, as expected, there was no difference in AKT or mTORC1 activation between L-TSC2-WT and -5A muscle (Fig. S6j). Thus, any potential effects of skeletal muscle mTORC1 on systemic insulin sensitivity would affect L-TSC2-WT and -5A mice to the same extent. These data further support that obesity-induced hyperinsulinemia is not a primary driver of hepatic mTORC1 activation and that an impairment in insulin-stimulated hepatic mTORC1 signaling does not grossly affect systemic glucose homeostasis under such conditions.

Glucagon is a suppressive signal of hepatic mTORC1 The present study has focused on the interplay between insulin and nutrients in the induction of hepatic mTORC1 upon feeding. However, whether there are speciﬁc signals that suppress hepatic mTORC1 activation during fasting, outside of a reduction in feeding-induced stimulatory signals, is unknown. To this end, the fasting hormone glucagon has been reported to inhibit mTORC1 in perfused rat liver and primary hepatocytes71–73, and forskolin, which recapitulates one aspect of glucagon signaling by increasing cAMP levels and activating protein kinase A (PKA), also suppresses mTORC1 in non-hepatic cell lines72,74. However, the potential contribution of glucagon to the suppression of hepatic mTORC1 during fasting has not been directly tested. In a time course experiment, we found that glucagon acutely suppresses mTORC1 signaling in primary mouse hepatocytes, with maximal inhibition at 30 minutes and sustained inhibition for at least 6 h (Fig. 7a). The induction of canonical glucagon signaling was con- ﬁrmed by the PKA-mediated phosphorylation of CREB. Additionally, acute glucagon treatment attenuated mTORC1 activation induced by insulin (Fig. 7b) or by siRNA-mediated knockdown of Tsc2 (Fig. 7c) in primary hepatocytes, suggesting a TSC complex-independent mechanism of suppression. We next took a genetic approach to evaluate the role of glucagon signaling in the regulation of hepatic mTORC1. Gcgrﬂ/ﬂmice were bred with mice expressing Albumin-Cre to generate mice with liver-speciﬁc knockout of the glucagon receptor (L-Gcgr-KO), as previously described75. We ﬁrst assessed whether the glucagon receptor (GCGR) is required for the suppression of mTORC1 in response to exogenous glucagon treatment using hepatocytes from L-Gcgr-KO or Gcgrﬂ/ﬂmice. Glucagon treatment had no effect on mTORC1 signaling in Gcgr−/−

hepatocytes, while forskolin, which activates the cAMP signaling cascade downstream of GCGR, suppressed mTORC1 signaling similarly in Gcgrﬂ/ﬂand L-Gcgr-KO hepatocytes, with corresponding effects on CREB phosphorylation (Fig. 7d). These data indicate that suppression of mTORC1 by glucagon is mediated through the hepatic GCGR. Discussion The liver coordinates systemic metabolism in response to physiological nutrient intake. The mTORC1 signaling network controls cellular metabolism and is sensitive to local and systemic nutrient status, with low pathway activation in the liver during fasting and acute induction in response to feeding. By mutating TSC2 at the ﬁve AKT-mediated phosphosites that are required for mTORC1 activation by insulin in

cells26,28,52, we generated the L-TSC2-5A mouse model as a genetic tool to deﬁne the speciﬁc contribution of insulin-AKT-TSC signaling to the physiological regulation of mTORC1 in the liver. Studies in mice with liver-speciﬁc TSC1 or TSC2 deletion demonstrate that the TSC complex is required for the dynamic regulation of hepatic mTORC1 by fasting and feeding, resulting in constitutively elevated mTORC1 signaling, even in the fasted state10,11,29. However, these models do not provide insight into the relevant physiological inputs integrated to control mTORC1 activation in this setting. AKT1/2 knockout mice have demonstrated that AKT is required for hepatic mTORC1 activation in response to insulin34,36. The ﬁndings described here provide mechanistic insights into this liver-intrinsic mechanism, demonstrating that insulin activates mTORC1 through AKT-mediated phosphorylation of the ﬁve sites on TSC2. As the mTORC1 response to insulin and glucose is signiﬁcantly decreased, but not entirely absent, from L- TSC2−5A livers, it is likely that other AKT-dependent mechanisms, such as phosphorylation of PRAS4016,17,76 or of other sites on TSC2, play an additional, more minor, role in this induction. Furthermore, other reported mechanisms of glucose sensing by mTORC1, such as Rag- and TSC complex-mediated mechanisms42,77–81 or through the glycolytic intermediate dihydroxyacetone phosphate (or DHAP)82, may also contribute in some settings. We conﬁrmed that feeding also robustly activates hepatic AKT, the AKT-mediated phosphorylation of TSC2, and mTORC1 signaling. However, our genetic data demonstrate that the AKT-TSC2 circuit is dispensable for the induction of hepatic mTORC1 signaling by feeding a normal chow diet. This ﬁnding, while surprising, is supported by previous studies showing that hepatic mTORC1 activation by feeding is intact in mice with liver-speciﬁc genetic deletion of the insulin receptor, which lack AKT activation35,83. We found that dietary protein is essential for hepatic mTORC1 induction by feeding regardless of TSC2 phosphorylation status. This ﬁnding is consistent with a previous report that the induction of hepatic mTORC1 signaling upon refeeding requires dietary leucine84. Furthermore, studies in mice expressing constitutively active RagA or lacking the leucine sensors Sestrin1 and Sestrin2 have provided genetic evidence that the amino acid sensing branch plays a critical role in hepatic mTORC1 regulation42,84–86. While many studies in immortalized cell lines have established that maximal mTORC1 activation requires both nutrient and growth

factor signaling6,8, our observations in the L-TSC2−5A mice suggest that insulin signaling may be dispensable for the activation of hepatic mTORC1, particularly in response to protein-rich diets. In fact, amino acids appear to be both necessary and sufﬁcient for near full mTORC1 activation in primary mouse hepatocytes, while the impact of insulin signaling through AKT and TSC2 phosphorylation was only observed under lower amino acid concentrations or, in the intact liver, when feeding a low protein diet. Given that plasma insulin levels were similar following chow and HC-LP diet feeding, we conclude that dietary protein is the primary factor determining the impact of insulin-AKT- TSC signaling in postprandial hepatic mTORC1 activation (Fig. 8). This hierarchical regulation of mTORC1 activation in the liver is in contrast to the model of signal integration established predominantly from cell culture models, where maximal mTORC1 activation appears to require both nutrients and growth factors (e.g., insulin)6,8. However, previous work found that feeding-induced mTORC1 activation is dependent on AKT-mediated TSC2 phosphorylation52 in muscle tissue. Thus, our data do not overturn this established model but indicate that not all tissues will completely ﬁt the existing model, with distinct tissues being adapted to the relevant physiological signals and unique metabolic functions of their respective organ system. For instance, the liver is particularly unusual in that it receives both insulin and nutrient signals directly from portal circulation and plays a major role in clearing both. It is important to note that our conclusions are largely limited to acute activation of hepatic mTORC1 and acknowledge that patterns of regulation may shift across a broader time course of feeding. This inconsistency may be due to differences in timing (25 min glucose gavage versus one-hour feeding). The distinct modalities of nutrient delivery—gavage versus voluntary feeding—may also lead to differences in nutrient absorption, stress responses, or induction of gut- or nervous system-derived signals. Interestingly, POMC neuron-mediated activation of the sympathetic nervous system reportedly induces hepatic mTORC1 in response to food perception in mice87, which may not occur upon oral gavage. Additionally, dietary sucrose, which is metabolized into glucose and fructose, maybe lesspotent for mTORC1 induction than a bolus of pure glucose. Indeed, fructose was found in an independent study to acutely suppress hepatic mTORC1 in mice88. Published studies suggest that the dynamic nature of mTORC1 signaling in insulin-responsive tissues, including the liver, is critical to whole-body metabolic homeostasis12,29,38. It has been

proposed that liver mTORC1 activation becomes elevated in obesity4,13,89 and contributes to hepatic insulin resistance, with in vitro studies implicating a variety of negative feedback mechanisms on insulin signaling13,45–47,49,50. However, the present study found no differences in hepatic mTORC1 activation between mice fed a high-fat versus a low-fat diet, despite overt impairments in glucose homeostasis and hyperinsulinemia. Interestingly, we did ﬁnd mTORC1 activation to be elevated in skeletal muscle tissue of diet-induced obese mice. One potential explanation for the discrepancy is that some previous studies utilized a chow diet to control for HFD12,13. Chow diets contain minimal sucrose and various whole food ingredients that semipuriﬁed diets do not, confounding the comparison between obese and lean mice in these studies. Interestingly, obesity in humans is associated with elevated levels of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs)90, which have been proposed to contribute to insulin resistance, at least in part, through liver and/or muscle mTORC1 activation90–92. Given our ﬁndings that dietary protein and amino acids are dominant for the activation of hepatic mTORC1, it is possible that a BCAA–mTORC1 axis drives metabolic impairments in obesity without the necessity of broad, persistent upregulation. Another possibility is that zonal regulation of hepatic mTORC1, which is not reﬂected in immunoblots of whole liver lysates, is impaired under conditions of obesity84,93,94. Our ﬁndings contradict the purported dogma that hepatic mTORC1 is chronically activated in obesity, emphasizing the need for further investigation into the causal role of mTORC1 in tissue insulin resistance and systemic metabolic dysfunction. In addition to investigating mechanisms of hepatic mTORC1 activation, we also evaluated glucagon, which inhibits mTORC1 in hepatocytes and perfused liver tissue71–73, as a potential mediator of hepatic mTORC1 suppression during fasting. We provide genetic evidence in support of hepatic mTORC1 regulation by glucagon in vivo. The mechanism of mTORC1 regulation by glucagon remains unclear but is dependent on the canonical glucagon receptor and appears to rely on cAMP signaling, as it is recapitulated by forskolin, and seems at least partly independent of the TSC complex72,74. Glucagon promotes amino acid catabolism in hepatocytes and liver tissue95, which may contribute to its inhibition of mTORC1. However, it is likely that several mechanisms contribute to mTORC1 suppression during fasting, including a decrease in stimulatory signals from circulating amino acids and insulin. The metabolic response to fasting, including upregulation of glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and ketogenesis, is impaired in L-Gcgr-KO mice96–99. Given that several of these processes are opposed by mTORC110,11,85, it is possible that aberrant mTORC1 signaling contributes to the impaired fasting response in L-Gcgr-KO mice, but this remains to be directly tested. Importantly, the regulation of glucagon secretion is defective in obese mice100, leading to diminished dynamic shifts in plasma ratios of glucagon to insulin, which could also contribute to aberrant mTORC1 regulation in metabolic disease. This study demonstrates that macronutrient composition inﬂuences hepatic mTORC1 activation, independent of insulin induction, which could have important implications for energy balance and metabolic health. Important follow-up studies include evaluating how dietary insights gleaned from this study can be translated into insights for human health. Interestingly, restriction of dietary protein or select amino acids is sufﬁcient to promote longevity and metabolic health101–104, and lifespan extension is maximal in mice fed a low protein, high carbohydrate diet105. There is some evidence that these beneﬁts of low protein diets are mediated by reduced mTORC1 signaling, including in the liver67,106. Additionally, not only total dietary protein content, but protein source has also been found to inﬂuence hepatic mTORC1 activation and metabolic dysfunction in rats107. Importantly, low protein consumption is linked to health beneﬁts in humans, including reduced cancer risk and all-cause mortality108. Understanding how physiological mTORC1 is regulated

Primary Hepatocyte Isolation and Culture Mice were anesthetized using a ketamine/xylazine solution at a dose of 100 µg/10 µg per gram body weight. Quantiﬁcation of plasma amino acids by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry The method used for quantifying the absolute concentrations of plasma amino acids in mice following feeding was adapted from a previously described protocol111. Blood was collected from the tail vein in EDTA tubes (Microvette® CB 300 EDTA K2E, Sarstedt) and centrifuged to separate plasma. Plasma was mixed at a 1:10 volume ratio with a −20 °C mixture of methanol:acetonitrile:water (40:40:20) and a stable isotope–labeled internal standard13c labeled yeast extract (Cambridge Isotope Laboratory, Andover, MA, ISO1). These internal standards, together with a library of external metabolite standards, enabled absolute quantiﬁcation across a wide dynamic range. The sample was vigorously vortexed and then centrifuged at 4 °C at 13,000×g for 10 min. 30 μl of the resulting supernatant was transferred to an HPLC vial, from which 5 μl was injected into the LC–MS system for analysis. Chromatographic separation was achieved using an XBridge BEH Amide XP Column (2.5 μm, 2.1 mm × 150 mm) with a guard column (2.5 μm, 2.1 mm × 5 mm) (Waters). The mobile phase consisted of water:acetonitrile 95:5 for mobile phase A and water:acetonitrile 20:80 for mobile phase B, both containing 10 mM ammonium acetate and 10 mM ammonium hydroxide. The elution linear gradient was as follows: 0–3 min, 100% B; 3.2–6.2 min, 90% B; 6.5–10.5 min, 80% B; 10.7–13.5 min, 70% B; 13.7–16 min, 45% B; and 16.5–22 min, 100% B, with a ﬂow rate of 0.3 ml/min. The autosampler temperature was maintained at 4 °C, and the injection volume was 5 μl. Needle wash was performed between samples using methanol:acetonitrile:water. The mass spectrometer used was a Q Exactive HF (Thermo Fisher), which scanned from 70 to 1000m/z with switching polarity and a resolution of 120,000. Metabolite identiﬁcation was based on accurate mass and retention time, conﬁrmed against external standard pools, using El- MAVEN (Elucidata). Quantiﬁcation was performed either by stable isotope dilution, where a labeled internal standard was available, or by external calibration curves for metabolites lacking an internal standard. This approach enabled robust and sensitive quantiﬁcation of amino acids in plasma, resolving concentrations from low nanomolar to high millimolar levels.

Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 10.0, and details about statistical tests applied for each panel are provided in the corresponding ﬁgure legends. For experiments comparing two groups, an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test was used. Experiments comparing two or more groups across conditions were analyzed by two-way ANOVA with Sidak’s multiple comparison test, unless otherwise noted in the ﬁgure legend. No assumptions were made regarding sample distribution or standard deviation, and non-parametric tests were used in cases where data did not pass one or more normality tests applied by GraphPad Prism. Each data point represents an individual value, and graphical data are presented as mean ± SD, unless otherwise noted in the ﬁgure legend. In cases where exact values are not provided in ﬁgure panels or legends, asterisks above comparisons indicate the degree of signiﬁcance as follows: *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001.

Feeding-induced muscle mTORC1 signaling regulates postprandial protein synthesis and endurance but not muscle size

Samuel C. Lapp,1,2 Krystle C. Kalafut,1,2 Madi Y. Cissé,1,2 Khaled Tighanimine,1,2 Dean M. Rosenthal,1,2 Will Doxsey,1 Sheng Hui,1 Karen E. Inouye,1 Claire E. Morrow,1,2 Yann Cormerais,1,2 and Brendan D. Manning1,2

1Department of Molecular Metabolism, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA.

Introduction Skeletal muscle is a crucial site for metabolic homeostasis (1, 2). It is the largest insulin-sensitive organ in healthy adults, the primary amino acid depot in mammals, and critical for locomotion (1–3). Skeletal muscle is uniquely plastic in response to diverse stimuli, including endocrine and growth factors, nutrients, and contraction, influencing muscle growth in a time- and intensity-dependent manner (1, 2, 4, 5). Dysregulation in signaling from these stimuli from inactivity, malnutrition, aging, cancer, or genetic disruption results in skeletal muscle weakness or atrophy (6–15). Therefore, understanding the dominant factors regulating skeletal muscle mass and function will inform us on better ways to address disease- or lifestyle-related muscle loss. Food intake provides a complex input of endocrine factors and nutrients that stimulate anabolism and suppress catabolism in skeletal muscle (3, 16, 17). These signals converge on the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 1 (mTORC1) in skeletal muscle to regulate, in part, this transition to net anabolism (16, 18). mTORC1 is a conserved regulator of cellular growth and critical for skeletal muscle mass (11–15, 19, 20). This protein complex consists of mTOR, lethal with SEC13 protein 8 (LST8), and regulatory-associated protein of mTOR (RAPTOR) as its essential core components (18). Ras homolog enriched in brain (RHEB) is a small GTPase that, when GTP-loaded, binds to and activates mTORC1 (21–23). Amino acids activate mTORC1 in a Rag GTPase-dependent manner by prompting the interaction of mTORC1 with GTP-bound RHEB (24–26). Hence, local amino acid availability is essential for mTORC1 activation. The GTP/GDP-loading state of RHEB is regulated by exogenous endocrine and growth factors, including insulin, through the tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) protein complex (21). The TSC complex, consisting of TSC1, TSC2, and TBC1D17, serves as a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) for RHEB, thus decreasing RHEB-GTP levels and inhibiting its activation of mTORC1 (21). Therefore, growth

Activation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex1 (mTORC1) promotes muscle protein synthesis, mass, and function. Muscle mTORC1 can be activated by feeding and contraction. Here, muscle mTORC1 signaling, protein synthesis, mass, and function are characterized in a genetic mouse model that separates these 2 major modes of muscle mTORC1 regulation. AKT signaling is required for feeding-induced muscle mTORC1 signaling and protein synthesis, and mice expressing a mutant of tuberous sclerosis complex 2 (TSC2) that cannot be phosphorylated by AKT specifically in skeletal muscle (SkM-TSC2-5A) attenuate these effects of feeding. Despite this loss of postprandial protein synthesis, SkM-TSC2-5A mice have similar muscle and myofiber size compared with SkM-TSC2-WT mice. SkM-TSC2-5A mice maintain normal muscle mTORC1 activation in response to contraction and exhibit no differences in atrophy-related gene expression or ribosomal content. SkM-TSC2-5A mice exhibit improved maximal endurance capacity without changes in muscle contractile function. This phenotype occurs without alterations in muscle glycogen content or myofiber type, but it does coincide with a modest increase in muscle mitochondrial content. Therefore, AKT-mediated phosphorylation of TSC2 is required for postprandial mTORC1 activation and the induction of protein synthesis; however, these are dispensable for the development and maintenance of muscle mass in sedentary mice.

factor activation of mTORC1 is thought to occur primarily through preventing the TSC complex from acting as a RHEB-GAP. Following insulin stimulation, the protein kinase AKT is activated and directly phosphorylates TSC2 on at least 5 sites, spatially separating it from RHEB and allowing RHEB-GTP to accumulate and activate mTORC1 (21, 27–29). However, nearly all these regulatory mechanisms upstream of mTORC1 are derived from studies in cell culture models. Unique among cell types, skeletal muscle cells comprising myofibers also activate mTORC1 by contraction (4, 30). While this regulation is less well understood than that coming from insulin, AKT and TSC2-dependent and -independent mechanisms have been proposed (15, 31–33). Thus, signals from endocrine factors, nutrients, and contraction may converge on mTORC1 in skeletal muscle, making the functional dissection of any individual input challenging. This current study seeks to isolate the role of endocrine signaling to mTORC1 in response to feeding and the physiological role of feeding in determining skeletal muscle mass and function. For this purpose, a skeletal muscle–specific mouse model expressing a mutant of TSC2 (SkM-TSC2-5A) that lacks the inhibitory AKT-mediated phosphorylation sites on TSC2, specifically in skeletal muscle, was generated. The TSC complex in the muscle of these mice is insensitive to inhibition by AKT but leaves other AKT functions and AKT-independent inputs to mTORC1 regulation intact. The SkM-TSC2-5A model demonstrates that these phosphorylation sites are required for postprandial induction of mTORC1 activation and protein synthesis in skeletal muscle. However, loss of postprandial protein synthesis did not reduce bodyweight, lean mass, muscle weight, or myofiber size in sedentary mice. Instead, this suggests that muscle size is likely maintained by alternative signals to mTORC1, such as contraction, which we show to be unaffected in SkM-TSC2-5A mice. Functionally, AKT signaling to mTORC1 is dispensable for the contractile properties of muscle, but its loss enhances maximal endurance capacity. This endurance phenotype is not due to changes in muscle glycogen content or fiber type proportions but is associated with a modest increase in muscle mitochondrial content. The findings described suggest that exogenous endocrine factor signaling induces postprandial mTORC1 activation and protein synthesis but that neither influence muscle mass nor contractile function in sedentary mice.

Results Feeding induces postprandial protein synthesis in skeletal muscle through activation of  AKT and mTORC1. There are multiple possible routes to muscle mTORC1 activation from feeding and contraction (Figure 1A). Studying cell signaling in mammalian tissues is challenging, especially in metabolic tissues such as skeletal muscle, where induction of the AKT-mTOR pathway and many other pathways is highly sensitive to the naturally differential timing of food intake. After piloting different conditions, including ad libitum feeding and daytime fast followed by night-time feed, we settled on an overnight fast followed by a 2-hour refeed as the best way to synchronize feeding behavior in mice to get more uniform, feeding-specific induction of the pathways of interest in skeletal muscle. Therefore, we use this paradigm throughout this study and recognize the caveats that accompany it. To assess how feeding stimulates mTORC1 signaling and protein synthesis in skeletal muscle, mice were fasted overnight and refed for 2 hours with or without an AKT inhibitor. Refeeding induced the activating phosphorylation of AKT and, with a trend toward significance, the AKT-mediated inhibitory phosphorylation of TSC2 in the quadriceps muscle (Figure 1, B and C, and Supplemental Figure 1A; supplemental material available online with this article; https://doi.org/10.1172/ jci.insight.210523DS1). This induction was associated with stimulation of mTORC1 signaling, as scored by phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 kinase 1 (S6K1) at T389, ribosomal protein S6 (S6) at S240/244, and eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E binding protein 1 (4E-BP1) (via electrophoretic shift) (Figure 1, B and D, and Supplemental Figure 1B). Pretreatment of mice with an AKT inhibitor reduced feeding-induced muscle TSC2 phosphorylation and mTORC1 signaling to that of the fasted state (Figure 1, B–D, and Supplemental Figure 1, A and B). Similarly, pretreatment with either an AKT inhibitor or the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin reduced both mTORC1 signaling and rates of postprandial protein synthesis to that of the fasted state (Figure 1, E and F), as determined by puromycin incorporation over the final 30 minutes of refeeding (34). Together, these data demonstrate that acute refeeding induces mTORC1 signaling and protein synthesis in a manner that is dependent on AKT. AKT-mediated phosphorylation of  TSC2 is required for feeding-induced activation of  mTORC1. AKT activates mTORC1, at least in part, through TSC2 phosphorylation in vitro and likely also in skeletal muscle (Figure 1A) (27, 35, 36). As confirmation of proper Cre-dependent recombination at these 2 loci, transcripts of the hTSC2 transgenes are detected only in the skeletal muscle of Cre+ SkM-TSC2-WT and -5A mice (Figure 2B). Reciprocally, endogenous mTsc2 transcripts were greatly decreased in Cre-expressing skeletal muscle relative to floxed controls. In contrast, both Cre+ and Cre– mice express similar levels of mTsc2 transcripts in control tissues, including the cardiac muscle and liver (Figure 2B). Given the documented expression of HSA-Cre in striated muscles (37), which include both skeletal and cardiac muscle, relative recombination was also assessed by measuring TSC2 phosphorylation at one of the sites mutated in the SkM-TSC2-5A mice, T1462, in the gastrocnemius and heart (Figure 2, C–E). SkM-TSC2-5A mice completely lack phosphorylation of TSC2 at T1462 in skeletal muscle but maintain comparable phosphorylation in the heart, confirming that expression of endogenous WT TSC2 is unchanged in the heart and that this model is skeletal muscle specific. When fed ad libitum, SkM-TSC2-5A mice trended toward higher levels of skeletal muscle AKT activation compared with SkM-TSC2-WT mice (Figure 2, F and G, and Supplemental Figure 2, A and B). Despite this, muscles from both male and female SkM-TSC2-5A mice showed a decrease in mTORC1 signaling (Figure 2, F and H, and Supplemental Figure 2, A and C). While there was no difference between male SkM-TSC2-WT and -5A mice in skeletal muscle AKT, S6, or 4E-BP1 phosphorylation following a 12-hour daytime fast, SkM-TSC2-5A mice had significantly elevated phosphorylation of AKT and abrogation of postprandial S6 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation following 2 hours of refeeding (Figure 2, I–K). The increased AKT activation in SkM-TSC2-5A muscles likely reflects loss of the well-documented mTORC1-mediated feedback inhibition of AKT signaling (39–41). Given that feeding increases nutrient availability, metabolomic analyses was performed on skeletal muscle following the same fasting and refeeding paradigm to determine whether major changes in skeletal muscle metabolites might underlie the dampened mTORC1 signaling in SkM-TSC2-5A muscle. Feeding induced an increase in some, but not all, amino acids present in the skeletal muscle, and SkM-TSC2-5A mice had similar or elevated levels of muscle amino acids compared with SkM-TSC2-WT mice (Supplemental Figure 2D). Both glycolytic and TCA cycle intermediates, as well as free fatty acid species, were also similar in the muscles of SkM-TSC2-WT and -5A mice under both fasting and feeding conditions (Supplemental Figure 2, E and F). The greater induction of postprandial protein synthesis in the muscles of 2-month-old mice may be indicative of the rapid growth occurring at this age (4, 11). At 6 months of age, there was no difference between male SkM-TSC2-WT and -5A mice in respiratory exchange ratio (RER) with ad libitum refeeding following the same fasting paradigm as above, suggesting that there are likely similar feeding habits and nutrient absorption between genotypes (Supplemental Figure 3E). These data demonstrate that AKT-mediated phosphorylation of TSC2 to activate mTORC1 is required for the induction of postprandial protein synthesis in skeletal muscle. AKT-mediated phosphorylation of  TSC2 has substrate specific effects downstream of  skeletal muscle mTORC1 signaling. mTORC1 has downstream substrates that fall into 1 of 4 categories: RHEB-dependent, rapamycin sensitive (e.g., S6K1); RHEB-dependent, partially rapamycin sensitive (e.g., 4E-BP1); RHEB-dependent, rapamycin resistant (e.g., unc-51 like autophagy activating kinase 1 [ULK1]); and RHEB-independent, rapamycin resistant (e.g., transcription factor EB [TFEB]) (42, 43). Therefore, it is critical to understand how specific inputs to mTORC1, like feeding, can selectively affect downstream substrates. Given that AKT-mediated phosphorylation of TSC2 should only affect the RHEB-dependent targets of mTORC1, the effects of feeding on the phosphorylation of S6K1, 4E-BP1, ULK1, and TFEB — representative of these 4 categories — were determined in the skeletal muscle of fasted and refed SkM-TSC2-WT and -5A mice. As seen above, the feeding-induced phosphorylation of skeletal muscle S6K1 and 4E-BP1 were abrogated in both male and female SkM-TSC2-5A mice (Figure 4, A, B, and E, and Supplemental Figure 4A). The feeding-induced mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of skeletal muscle ULK1 at S757 was also significantly decreased in SkM-TSC2-5A mice (Figure 4, A, C, and F, and Supplemental Figure 4A). In contrast, the mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of the TFEB transcription factor, which is dependent on amino acid signaling through the Rag proteins and independent of TSC-RHEB signaling (44), was not impaired in SkM-TSC2-5A muscle but was actually elevated, especially in male mice (Figure 4, A, D, and G, and Supplemental Figure 4A). This difference in TFEB phosphorylation is consistent with increased TSC2 activity yielding a decrease in RHEB-dependent mTORC1 signaling in SkM-TSC2-5A muscles, as the RHEB-mediated activation of mTORC1 has been found to hinder the ability of mTORC1 to regulate TFEB (45–47). These data suggest that AKT-mediated phosphorylation of TSC2 in skeletal muscle is required specifically for postprandial RHEB-mTORC1 signaling to downstream substrates but not regulation of RHEB-independent substrates of mTORC1, like TFEB. AKT-mediated phosphorylation of  TSC2 does not affect skeletal muscle expression of  atrophy-related genes or RNA content. Alterations in muscle mass can come from changes in the relative balance of protein synthesis and degradation (2). Atrophy-related genes encode proteins that induce muscle protein degradation and whose transcripts are elevated during muscle atrophy (48–51). The most relevant of these are the ubiquitin ligases F-box only protein 3 (Fbxo32, also known as Atrogin-1) and tripartite motif containing 63 (Trim63, also known as MuRF1), as well as growth arrest and DNA damage-inducible 45 (Gadd45a) (50, 52–54). However, no significant differences in transcript levels of any of these genes were detected between SkM-TSC2-WT and -5A muscles under fasting or ad libitum–fed conditions (Figure 6, A and B). These data suggest that a decrease in muscle protein degradation, at least due to differential expression of these common atrophy-related genes, is unlikely to explain the maintenance of muscle mass in the SkM-TSC2-5A mice. Overall protein synthetic capacity and cellular growth are dictated by ribosomal content, which can be regulated by mTORC1 (55). Muscle mass scales has a positive, linear relationship with ribosomal content, which is considered reflective of total RNA content (4, 56, 57). This suggests that loss of feeding-induced muscle mTORC1 signaling does not affect ribosomal content in skeletal muscle, implying that both genotypes have similar protein synthetic capacity in their muscles. AKT-mediated phosphorylation of  TSC2 is dispensable for contraction-mediated mTORC1 activation in skeletal muscle. While skeletal muscle growth requires mTORC1 activation, the relative contribution of upstream signals, including feeding and contraction, to growth-promoting mTORC1 signaling are less well understood. Since the SkM-TSC2-5A mice are defective in feeding-induced mTORC1 activation without effects on muscle mass, contraction-induced mTORC1 signaling was assayed in these mice. Thus, maximal intensity contractions (MIC) were elicited through direct electrical stimulation of the sciatic nerve (Figure 7A), as previously described (58). At 3 hours after contraction, when skeletal muscle mTORC1 signaling has been shown to peak in response to MIC (30), there was no difference in AKT activation, as previously described (59), or its phosphorylation of TSC2 between the contracted (MIC) and uncontracted contralateral (Cntrl) TA muscle from the same mouse in both males and females (Figure 7, B, C, and E, and Supplemental Figure 6, A and B). These data suggest that contraction does not activate muscle mTORC1 through AKT-mediated phosphorylation of TSC2 and that the sustained ability of contraction to stimulate mTORC1 may be an alternative signal that contributes to the development and maintenance of normal muscle mass in SkM-TSC2-5A mice. We next assessed endurance capacity via run-to-exhaustion experiments as previously described (62). Mice ran at a consistent incline with periodic increases in treadmill speed until exhaustion. Interestingly, male SkM-TSC2-5A mice showed improved endurance capacity, as demonstrated by increased maximum speed, total run time, and cumulative distance run (Figure 8, J–L). However, this phenotype was not observed in female SkM-TSC2-5A mice (Supplemental Figure 7, F–H). Thus, parameters that might underlie this unexpected phenotype were measured in muscles from male mice. Improved endurance capacity in SkM-TSC2-5A mice is not associated with changes in skeletal muscle glycogen content. During maximal exercise, skeletal muscle energy production becomes disproportionally dependent on glycogen (63), suggesting that increased glycogen content may explain differences in endurance capacity between SkM-TSC2-WT and -5A mice. In metabolic cage measurements, SkM-TSC2-5A mice exhibited a slightly higher, but not statistically significant, RER — particularly when having access to wheel running, perhaps indicative of higher carbohydrate utilization (Figure 9A). This prompted us to investigate alterations in glycogen and glucose metabolism. SkM-TSC2-5A mice have enhanced feeding-induced AKT activation in their skeletal muscle compared with SkM-TSC2-WT mice (Figure 2, G and J and Figure 9, B and C). GSK3β is a direct target inhibited by AKT that has been implicated in regulating glycogen content through its inhibition of glycogen synthase (35). Indeed, the AKT-mediated inhibitory phosphorylation of GSK3β was elevated during refeeding in SkM-TSC2-5A muscles compared with WT (Figure 9, B and D), which could theoretically result in increased glycogen synthesis in these muscles. However, SkM-TSC2- WT and -5A mice did not exhibit significant differences in glycogen content or GSK3β phosphorylation in muscles from ad libitum fed (Figure 9E and Supplemental Figure 8, A–C) or fasted (Figure 9, B, D, and F) mice. Thus, an increase in muscle glycogen content is unlikely to explain improvements in endurance capacity in SkM-TSC2-5A mice. A primary function of insulin-stimulated AKT signaling in skeletal muscle is to promote glucose uptake and clearance from the blood (1). Therefore, we investigated glucose clearance and insulin sensitivity in SkM-TSC2-WT and -5A mice. There were no differences in either ad libitum or fasted blood glucose levels between male SkM-TSC2-WT and -5A mice (Supplemental Figure 8, D and E). Glucose tolerance tests (GTT) in both male and female mice also showed no differences between genotypes in glucose clearance (Supplemental Figure 8, F–I). Likewise, there were no differences in insulin sensitivity in insulin-tolerance tests (ITT) between genotypes in either male or female cohorts (Supplemental Figure 8, J–M). Together, we observe no overt differences in glucose metabolism dependent on AKT-mediated phosphorylation of TSC2 in skeletal muscle. SkM-TSC2-5A muscle display a moderate increase in mitochondrial content without changes in muscle fiber type. Beyond glycogen content, skeletal muscle fiber type and mitochondrial content can alter endurance capacity (64–66). Skeletal muscle fiber types exist on a gradient between oxidative (I and IIA) and glycolytic (IIX and IIB), where a shift toward more oxidative fibers is associated with improved endurance capacity (65). Complete ablation of skeletal muscle mTORC1 signaling has been found to result in a shift toward type I and IIA fiber types (13, 61); therefore, fiber type identity was compared between muscles of SkM-TSC2-WT and -5A mice. Skeletal muscle gene expression for markers of oxidative (Tnni1, Myh1, Myh2) and glycolytic (Tnni2, Myh4) fiber types did not significantly differ between SkM-TSC2-WT and -5A mice (Figure 10, A and B). Discussion The SkM-TSC2-5A mice provide insights into the physiological regulation and function of skeletal muscle mTORC1, which is widely believed to be a key signaling node in the control of muscle growth and strength (4, 16). While the complete absence or maximal sustained activation of skeletal muscle mTORC1 — as achieved through muscle-specific genetic deletion of RAPTOR or TSC1, respectively — has dramatic effects on skeletal muscle mass (12, 13), the SkM-TSC2-5A mice demonstrate that abrogation of a single key regulatory input into mTORC1, from feeding, has specific effects on muscle function without altering muscle mass. The SkM-TSC2-5A model separates feeding-induced mTORC1 activation and postprandial protein synthesis from muscle mass and function. While previous studies implicate AKT-mediated activation of mTORC1 as crucial for muscle mass development (2, 20), the SkM-TSC2-5A model provides genetic evidence that decreased AKT-mediated mTORC1 activation and the subsequent loss of postprandial protein synthesis does not alter skeletal muscle mass. Despite the evidence provided here that mTORC1-mediated protein synthesis in response to refeeding is dispensable for muscle mass, mTORC1 is undeniably required during phases of rapid muscle growth, such as during development and mechanical loading-induced hypertrophy (13, 15, 58, 61). Therefore, mTORC1-dependent maintenance of muscle mass in SkM-TSC2-5A mice may occur through sustained contraction-mediated mTORC1 activation or other alternative signals beyond those derived just after food intake. In support of this hypothesis, SkM-TSC2-5A mice maintain sensitivity to contraction-mediated mTORC1 activation. Furthermore, rates of protein synthesis do not significantly differ between genotypes in the fasted state, indicating that signals outside of feeding-induced mTORC1 maintain skeletal muscle protein synthesis in other contexts. Feeding-induced mTORC1 activation and protein synthesis may instead be critical for skeletal muscle growth through synergizing with other signals. In support of this, feeding in combination with contraction potently increases muscle protein synthesis and hypertrophy relative to feeding alone (5, 68). Nutrient intake is clearly essential for both the maintenance and growth of muscle (3), but the effects of acute refeeding on mTORC1 do not appear essential for either. While acute feeding activates mTORC1 via AKT, AKT has functions independent of mTORC1 that can contribute to the control of muscle mass (1, 11). In summary, this study shows that acute feeding–induced muscle mTORC1 signaling and protein synthesis are dependent on AKT-mediated phosphorylation of TSC2 in skeletal muscle. However, we provide genetic evidence muscle protein synthesis induced just after feeding does not determine muscle mass or strength in sedentary mice. AKT-mediated regulation of the TSC complex and mTORC1 may have a negative effect on skeletal muscle mitochondrial content through an undetermined mechanism, and the loss of mTORC1 regulation through this signal improves endurance capacity in male mice.

Limitations of this study While no changes in heart TSC2 phosphorylation or mass were observed in SkM-TSC2-5A mice, HSA-Cre has been found to express in all striated muscle tissues, including the heart (37). Whole-body TSC2-5A mice, produced with CMV-Cre, lack TSC2 phosphorylation in the heart and have reduced heart mass, further supporting that the model described here is skeletal muscle specific (36). Signaling was assessed primarily at 2 hours of refeeding, a time point that might be too long for some acute signaling events and too short for other downstream outcomes, including transcriptional regulation, to be detected (71). While the experimental paradigm used throughout was designed to reproducibly detect acute changes in skeletal muscle signaling and protein synthesis induced specifically by food consumption across a cohort of mice, it does not represent the more physiological ad libitum context in which muscle mass and function are assessed. Skeletal muscle was lysed in TRIzol (Invitrogen, 15596018) on ice, and RNA was isolated following manufacturer’s instructions. RNA was reverse transcribed using the Advanced cDNA Synthesis Kit (Bio-Rad, 1725038). qPCR analysis was performed with technical triplicates using iTaq SYBR green (Bio-Rad, 172-5124) and the Quant Studio 7 Flex Real-Time PCR System. Primer sequences included the following: Fbxo32: TTCTCGACTGCCATCCT, ATGCCACTCAGGGATGT; Gadd45α: ATTACGGTCGGCGTGTA, GATGAGGGTGAAATGGATCTG; Myh1: CGGAGTCAGGTGAATACTCACG, GAGCATGAGCTAAGGCACTCT; Myh2: ACTTTGG- CACTACGGGGAAAC, CAGCAGCATTTCGATCAGCTC; Myh4: AAACCACCTCAGAGTTGTGGA, GTTCCGAAGGTTCCTGATTGC; Tnni1: GATGGGAGATGAGGAGAAGC, GGGCAGTGTTCT- GACAGGTA; Tnni2: GGCCTCTGAGCACAGAAAGT, GCCGGGAGCTATCTTTCTTA; Trim63: GAGAACCTGGAGAAGCAGCT, CCGCGGTTGGTCCAGTAG; Tsc2: GCATGCAGTTCTCACCT- TAT, GGGTAGTCCTTGATCACTTTG; TSC2: GGCTCTATTCTCTCAGGAACTC, GATGGACAG- GACGATCTCATAG; and 36B4: AGATGCAGCAGATCCGCAT, GTTCTTGCCCATCAGCACC. Metabolite extraction and LC-MS analysis in skeletal muscle. Adapted from Hui et al. (75). In brief, whole, flash-frozen quadriceps were pulverized using a Cryomill (Retsch) until forming a fine powder. In total, 20 mg of tissue was resuspended in ice-cold metabolite-extraction buffer (methanol/acetonitrile/water at 40:40:20 volume ratio) at a 25 mg/mL ratio. Samples were vortexed and incubated for 10 minutes on ice, centrifuged at 1,000g for 5 minutes at 4°C. In total, 500 μL of supernatant was aliquoted into a new tube and centrifuged at 21,000g for 10 minutes at 4°C. Supernatant was transferred to an HPLC vial, from which 5 μL were injected into the LC-MS. Chromatographic separation was achieved using Vanquish UHPLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and XBridge BEH Amide XP column (2.5 μm, 2.1 mm × 150 mm) with guard column (2.5 μm, 2.1 mm × 5 mm) (Waters). The mobile phase A was water/acetonitrile 95:5, and the mobile phase B was water/acetonitrile 20:80, with both phases containing 10 mM ammonium acetate and 10 mM ammonium hydroxide. The elution linear gradient was: 0–3 minutes, 100% B; 3.2–6.2 minutes, 90% B; 6.5–10.5 minutes, 80% B; 10.7–13.5 minutes, 70% B; 13.7–16 minutes, 45% B; and 16.5–22 minutes, 100% B, with flow rate of 0.3 mL/min. The autosampler was at 4°C, with the injection volume of 5 μL. Between-samples needle wash (methanol/acetonitrile/water at 40:40:20) was used. Samples were analyzed using an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and scanned from 70 to 1000 m/z with switching polarity. The resolution was 120,000. Metabolites were identified based on accurate mass and retention time using EI-Maven (Elucidata) with our in-house library. Relative metabolite abundance was determined by total ion counts across conditions. Indirect calorimetry and behavioral assessments. Mice were housed individually in cages inside Environmental Control Cabinets (Sable Systems #CAB-16 L_Y), set at 21°C, with lights on from 07:00 to 19:00 hours, and chamber humidity at 43%–63%. The following was measured using the Sable Promethion CORE Metabolic and Behavioral Analysis System: oxygen consumption (VO2), carbon dioxide production (VCO2), RER, energy expenditure (EE), wheel running, food intake, water intake, bodyweight, and locomotor activity. Mice were acclimated to the cages for 5 days prior to analysis with 1 day of acclimation connected to the system. Mice were assessed for 6 days with 3 days of wheel access followed by 3 days without wheel access. Afterward, mice underwent a 16-hour overnight fast (17:00–09:00) followed by ad libitum access to food to assess substrate utilization and eating habits under the conditions of protein synthesis experiments. Body composition was assessed before and after each study. Data were assessed using the CalR application (76).

Immunostaining of  skeletal muscle cross-sections. Skeletal muscles were dissected and immediately frozen in Tissue-Tek O.C.T. Compound (Sakura, 4583) in isopentane cooled in liquid nitrogen for 10–30 seconds depending on muscle size. Samples were immediately placed on dry ice then transferred to –80°C for storage. Frozen tissues were transferred on dry ice to –20°C cryostat for 1 hour (Microtome HM 505N Cryostat). Muscle samples were cut transversely at the midbelly. Serial sections were collected at 10 μm thickness onto Superfrost microscope slides (VWR; 48311-703) and stored at –80°C until staining. Slides were dried for 30 minutes at RT. Slides were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 minutes at 4°C. Slides were washed 3 times for 5 minutes in 1X PBS. Heat-induced antigen retrieval (HIAR) was performed in 1-L 10mM citrate buffer (0.5 mL Tween 20, pH 7). Slides were placed in warmed citrate buffer and maintained at a low boil for 10 minutes. Citrate buffer was diluted by consistent running of distilled water for 10 minutes. Slides were placed in permeabilization buffer (0.1M glycine, 0.1% Triton-X, syringe filtered in 1X PBS) for 10 minutes, followed by blocking buffer (5% goat serum [Jackson ImmunoResearch; 005-000-121], 2% bovine serum albumin [Sigma-Aldrich; A9647], 1:40 Mouse on Mouse blocking reagent [Vector Laboratories; MKB-2213-1], in 1X PBS, syringe filtered) for 1 hour at RT. Slides were incubated overnight at 4°C with the following: Alexa Fluor 594–conjugated wheat germ agglutinin (WGA, Thermo Fisher; W11262), myosin heavy chain Type I (BA-D5 [IgG2b]; concentrate, Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank; 1:500), Type IIA (SC-71 [IgG1]; concentrate, Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank; 1:1000), and Type IIB (BF-F3 [IgM]; concentrate, Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank; 1:200). Slides were washed 3 times for 5 minutes each in 1X PBS, incubated for 1 hour at RT with Alexa Fluor 568 anti-Mouse IgG2b (Jackson ImmunoResearch; 115-575-207), Alexa Fluor 488 Goat anti-Mouse IgM, μ-chain specific (Jackson ImmunoResearch; 115-545-075), and DyLight 405 anti-Mouse IgG1 (Jackson ImmunoResearch; 115-475-205). Slides were washed 3 times for 5 minutes with 1X PBS, mounted with VectaShield Hardset (Vector Laboratories; H-1400-10). Slides were incubated at RT for 30 minutes and were then sealed with clear nail polish. Slides were imaged with a Nikon Eclipse Ti microscope using an X-Cite 120LED lamphouse. Images were captured on an ANDOR Zyla 5.5 SCMOS camera using NIS-Elements software. All images were captured at 10x magnification under 20% iris intensity. Images of whole cross-sections were taken with 15% overlap and stitched together using NIS-Elements software. Whole plantaris muscles were analyzed; uniform areas of red gastrocnemius directly adjacent and lateral to the plantaris measuring 2 × 106 ± 4.3 × 103 μm2 per section were analyzed. Brightness of images was uniformly adjusted for analysis. CSA of fiber types were assessed with semiautomated muscle analysis using segmentation of histology (SMASH) in a blinded fashion (77). Fibers were manually outlined as needed, and all Type I fibers were manually outlined due to fluorophore overlap. Images were analyzed with the following parameters, pixel size 0.658 μm/pixel, minimum fiber area 300 μm2, maximum fiber area 8000 μm2, maximum eccentricity 0.97, and minimum convexity 0.7. Myofibers damaged from processing, overlapping myofibers, incomplete myofibers, and nonmyofiber selections were manually removed from SMASH analysis. Both gastrocnemius and plantaris were censored following sample loss (n = 1/group). Three-month-old male mice were fasted for 2.5 hours prior to procedure. Mice were anesthetized using 4% isoflurane and maintained with ~1% isoflurane via nosecone. Lidocaine (2 mg/kg bodyweight) was injected at the site of the incision. A small incision and blunt dissection tools were used to identify the sciatic nerve. Electrodes were placed transversely across the sciatic nerve and stimulated at 100 Hz with 0.5 ms pulses at 5V (Aurora Scientific, 1300A 3-in-1: Whole-Animal System) for a total of 10 sets of 6 contractions (58). Between each pulse, the leg was manually returned to the starting position by the experimenter. The wound was sealed, and mice were returned to cages without food. Functional strength assessments in mice. Inverted screen test and grip strength were measured as previously described (62, 78). Unacclimated mice were placed in the center of a wire screen that was inverted to suspend the mice approximately 35 cm above soft bedding. Time from inversion to fall was recorded. Grip strength was measured using a wire rack force meter (Chatillon, DFE-002), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In vivo force and fatigue measurement. 3-month-old male mice were anesthetized using 4% isoflurane and maintained with ~1% isoflurane via nosecone. Mice were placed supine on heat-support while platform was adjusted so the tibia was perpendicular to the foot plate with the leg extended and foot in a relaxed position (Aurora Scientific, 1300A 3-in-1: Whole-Animal System). The foot was secured in the mouse foot plate with surgical tape, and the leg was secured at the knee. For stimulation of the plantarflexors, electrodes were inserted transversely across the proximal region of the peroneal nerve. Isometric contractions were induced via biphasic stimulation first at 50 Hz, then 100 Hz, and 150 Hz as indicated for a 1-second tetanus with 1-minute rest between stimulations. After another minute of rest, fatigue was measured by 50 Hz stimulations for 1-second tetanus and 1-second rest for 150 contractions. Force was recorded for each contraction using accompanying software. Treadmill running. Maximal treadmill running was adapted from a previous study (62). In brief, mice were acclimated for 3 days at 5 m/min for 10 minutes at a 0° incline (Columbus Instruments, Exer-3/6). On the fourth day, mice ran at a 5° incline at 10 m/min for 10 minutes, followed by an increase of 2 m/min every 5 minutes until exhaustion. On the day of experiment, experimenter was blinded to genotype during each run. Exhaustion was defined by the inability to keep hindlimbs off the electric grid for > 5 seconds, at which point, the experiment was terminated, and animals were returned to their cages. Glycogen assessment. Skeletal muscle glycogen was measured using the Glycogen-Glo assay (Promega, catalog J5051) according to manufacturer’s instructions with the following adaptations. Approximately 15 mg of pulverized skeletal muscle was weighed and lysed in HCl supplemented with 0.2% Triton X-100 resulting in samples of equal concentration of tissue and allowed to rotate at 4°C for 2 hours to ensure full digestion. Samples were centrifuged at 4,500g for 5 minutes, and supernatant was diluted 1:5. Liver tissue samples and kit-provided standards were used as positive controls. GTT and ITT. Mice were fasted for 6 hours during the early light phase (08:00–14:00) with ad libitum access to water. For GTT, mice were subjected to i.p. injection with glucose in sterile saline (2 g/kg bodyweight). For ITT, mice were subjected to intraperitoneal injection with insulin in sterile saline (0.5 U/kg bodyweight in 0.1% protease-free BSA [HumulinR, Eli Lily]). Blood glucose was monitored periodically as noted using Contour Next EZ gluocometer (Bayer). Mitochondrial content. Mitochondrial content was assessed as previously described (67). Flash frozen quadriceps were pulverized using a Cryomill (Retsch) until forming a fine powder. mtDNA and nDNA was isolated using DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (Qiagen, catalog 69504) following manufacturer’s instructions using ~25 mg of tissue. Samples were normalized by total DNA content; then, copy number was assessed using qPCR as described above using the following primers (5′-3′): 16S: CCGCAAGGGAAAGATGAAAGAC, TCGTTTGGTTTCG- GGGTTTC; HK2: GCCAGCCTCTCCTGATTTTAGTGT, GGGAACACAAAAGACCTCTTCTGG; and ND1: CTAGCAGAAACAAACCGGGC, CCGGCTGCGTATTCTACGTT. Statistics. Statistical analysis was performed using Prism 11.0.1 software. For comparisons between 2 groups, a Mann-Whitney U test was performed. For comparisons between slopes, a 2-tailed t test was performed. For comparisons of 3 or more independent groups, an ordinary 1-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparisons was performed. For comparisons with 2 independent factors, a 2-way ANOVA with Holm-Šídák multiple comparisons was performed. For multiple independent comparisons between groups, multiple Mann-Whitney U tests with a Holm-Šídák correction were performed. All paired tests were performed 2 sided. Samples were censored in the following experiments: Figure 1F (n = 1) and Figure 3D (n = 2), when puromycin labeling was not detected indicating a technical failure in puromycin administration. Subject was censored from body composition due to premature death (Figure 5C and Supplemental Figure 5, C and E; n = 1). Subjects were censored from inverted screen test for climbing around and above the screen (Figure 8, E and F; n = 3). Subjects were censored from fatigue measures due to electrode displacement during experiment (Figure 8G and Supplemental Figure 6E; n = 1). P < 0.05 was considered significant. P > 0.05 and below 0.5 are reported. P values above 0.5 are not reported. Study approval.
